source.title: Reshaping Representation Space to Balance the Safety and Over-rejection in Large Audio Language Models
source.authors: Hao Yang; Li-Zhen Qu; Ehsan Shareghi; G. Haffari

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results for a deep fine-tuning strategy that aligns more than the first response token, bearing on V7, in large audio-language models. The modality and evaluation setting differ from the original work.
record.gate_note: The study also reports RRS fine-tuning results on harmful-response rates; those results do not measure whether safety is spread beyond the first response tokens, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Its t-SNE plots, feature-selection proportions, and cited findings do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study runs Qi et al. (2025)'s deep safety SFT, with the prefill range cut to 0–10, on three Qwen audio-language models. It reports harmful-question ASR and over-rejection against vanilla and first-token-only (shallow) SFT. That is a result on V7 in a new setting (audio LALMs), so T3 rather than T2. ASR is measured only on plain harmful questions, with no prefill or attack evaluation. So the study shows what deep training costs and achieves for plain refusal, but not whether depth adds robustness.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that RRS improves LALM safety in all three input modes, with ASR competitive with or better than the best SFT baseline and the best NSI, while raising ORR by only 0.88% on average. They also find that SFT-deep gives the strongest safety gain on Qwen-Audio but the highest ORR across all models. They chose shallow-mirror SFT as the best SFT baseline. They note that jailbreaks and adversarial audio attacks remain risks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses audio-language models and BeaverTails-derived audio data; its deep SFT condition is described as implementing Qi et al. (2025), with the prefill-token range reduced to 0 to 10. Its main proposed method is representation-space fine-tuning, not the original harmful fine-tuning or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports changes across modality modes and between fine-tuning strategies. Its feature-selection sweep finds ASR decreases as more safety features are selected while ORR generally increases.

fits_no_version.finding: RRS lowers harmful-response ASR across input modes for the three Qwen LALMs with small ORR increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-space fine-tuning can improve safety on plain harmful questions in audio-language models with little over-rejection.

fits_no_version.finding: First-token-only SFT (shallow-mirror) reaches ASR comparable to deep SFT on plain harmful questions with much lower ORR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On plain harmful questions, aligning only the first response token gives most of the refusal gain of deep alignment at lower over-rejection.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The evaluation is limited to three Qwen LALMs and plain harmful questions; the authors note that audio jailbreaking and adversarial attacks may remain risks. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the relevant results.
record.rows_left_out: Other SFT strategies and RRS ablations are not listed as V7 rows because they do not test whether safety is spread beyond the first response tokens. RRS ASR outcomes are recorded under fits_no_version. The study's feature-selection sweeps and t-SNE visualizations are not results for the listed versions.

untested.parts: Whether deep training holds up against prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding attacks or later fine-tuning. No per-position measure of how far safety extends. Plain-question ASR cannot separate deep from shallow alignment: first-token-only SFT reaches similar ASR.
No benign fine-tuning erosion test. Modality-adaptation degradation is only cited.
No prefill, suffix or decoding bypass tests.
Selects representation features, not weights or ranks.
No test of causes of shallowness.

missing.what: SFT-deep ASR for Qwen2-Audio (audio-text 28.11→2.51, text 10.93→1.31, audio-only 6.17→1.43) and Qwen2.5-Omni (10.0→1.94, 13.09→2.97, 8.63→2.46)
SFT-deep ORR for Qwen2-Audio (1.31→16.69) and Qwen2.5-Omni (1.66→34.23), plus Avg. NSI for SFT-deep (−47.08, −2.06, −24.45)
Shallow first-token SFT (mirror/parallel) ASR and ORR as the comparator to deep SFT

record.verdict_notes: The verdicts rest only on plain harmful-question ASR. The study never tests prefill or attack robustness, the core of V7. The deep recipe was altered (prefill range 0–10) and paired with a weight-penalty term. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fine-tune on harmful examples that elicit compliance.
The study does not test ordinary benign instruction fine-tuning as a cause of increased harmful compliance.
It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence across response positions.
It does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
It selects representation features, not a small set of weights or ranks carrying safety behaviour.
It does not test whether the data or objective causes safety shallowness.
It tests a deep fine-tuning strategy and reports behaviour, but does not directly measure how safety is distributed across response positions or whether the effect holds against adversarial attacks.

relationships.condition: All three Qwen LALMs, SFT-deep, AIAH plain harmful questions, all input modes
relationships.reason: Deep SFT cuts ASR sharply: Qwen-Audio 56.65→0.34 and 19.49→1.26 (r1, r2), with similar drops on Qwen2-Audio and Qwen2.5-Omni (Table 2, not in rows). Only plain refusal is shown; shallow SFT does about as well.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success fell sharply, for Qwen-Audio from 56.65 to 0.34 and from 19.49 to 1.26, with similar drops on Qwen2-Audio and Qwen2.5-Omni. Only plain refusal was tested, and shallow SFT did about as well.

relationships.condition: All three Qwen LALMs, SFT-deep, AIAH benign questions
relationships.reason: Deep SFT gives the highest over-rejection: Qwen-Audio 1.14→85.49 (r3), Qwen2-Audio 1.31→16.69, Qwen2.5-Omni 1.66→34.23 (Table 2). Net safety improvement is negative on all three (−47.08, −2.06, −24.45).
relationships.display_finding: Over-rejection rose from 1.14 to 85.49 on Qwen-Audio, 1.31 to 16.69 on Qwen2-Audio and 1.66 to 34.23 on Qwen2.5-Omni, giving negative net safety improvement on all three (−47.08, −2.06, −24.45).

relation.reason: Deep SFT receives its own evaluation in Table 2; the study does more than use or cite the method.

tranche.reason: The study implements modified deep safety SFT in the new setting of audio-language models and reports its safety outcomes alongside shallow SFT controls.

source_check.notes: Deep SFT uses Mirror with prefill lengths 0–10 and is evaluated on plain harmful questions; adversarial durability and positional safety spreading are untested. The substantial over-rejection cost should remain recorded separately from the safety-effect state.

statements.correction: Qwen-Audio SFT-deep: benign ORR 1.14% → 85.49%; audio-text ASR 56.65% → 0.34%; text-only ASR 19.49% → 1.26%. Utility cost observed; reversal or failure of the safety effect not established.
statements.problem: The over-rejection increase is accurate, but a utility cost alone does not establish limits_scope under the stated V7, which does not promise preserved benign compliance.
